study.title: Matthew 10 The mission of the twelve, the opposition and the reward of discipleship
study.overview: Matthew 10 records the sending of the twelve disciples as apostles, that is, sent with authority given by Jesus to announce the arrival of the Kingdom, serve in favor of the sick, and distinguish the gratuitousness of the gospel from any interested gain. The chapter also prepares the disciples for rejection, courts, division within families and persecution, showing that following Christ requires faithfulness above human bonds, without fear of men, but with reverence to God. The outcome of the teaching emphasizes that welcoming the messengers of Jesus is to welcome Christ Himself, and even the slightest gesture of support given to a disciple will be remembered by God as worthy of reward.

outline.title: Called and appointment of the twelve
outline.explanation: Jesus calls the twelve, gives them authority over unclean spirits and infirmities, and presents them nominally. The list shows that the mission is born from the sovereign choice of Christ and that the apostles are officially sent as representatives of him.

outline.title: Instructions for mission between Israel
outline.explanation: The twelve must first go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, proclaim the closeness of the Kingdom and act without seeking profit. They must depend on God's provision, seek worthy people, offer peace, and accept rejection as a sign of stricter judgment than that of Sodom and Gomorrah.

outline.title: Persecution, testimony and correct fear
outline.explanation: Jesus announces intense opposition: courts, floggings, family betrayals, and hatred because of his name. Still, he promises the help of the Spirit, calls the disciples to persevere to the end, teaches prudence without fear, and corrects the focus of fear: they must not fear who kills the body, but to God, who has authority over soul and body.

outline.title: Confess Christ and receive his little ones
outline.explanation: The public confession of Jesus before the people brings recognition before the Father; denying it brings denial to the Father. Discipleship can divide to the nearest house, requires supreme love for Christ and take the cross, but also receives the promise of reward for those who welcome prophets, righteous and even the smallest disciples with simple acts of support, like a glass of cold water.

study.context: The chapter fits the initial sending of the twelve disciples as apostles, that is, sent authorized by Jesus. The notes highlight that the number twelve is not accidental, as it refers to the twelve tribes of Israel and suggests the formation of a new people of God under the reign of the Messiah. The mission here is first directed to Israel, with the announcement that the Kingdom of Heaven is near. The notes also show that Jesus anticipates future persecution, especially when the commission of the disciples would widen after his resurrection. As for Matthew 10:23, there is interpretive uncertainty as to whether the coming of the Son of man points to his final turn or to a coming in judgment linked to the rejection suffered by the disciples.
study.theology: Matthew 10 unites authority, mission, suffering, and reward. Jesus is the Lord who sends, empowers and defines the scope of the message; the disciples do not act on their own initiative, but as representatives of it. The gospel is proclaimed as a gift received by grace and offered for free, which excludes religious exploitation. The chapter also teaches that the Kingdom of God does not eliminate immediate opposition; rather, authentic discipleship can bring conflict, even within the family. There is a clear hierarchy of allegiance: Christ is above the deepest bonds on earth. At the same time, God cares for his servants in detail, knows his sufferings, tells even the hairs of his head and values apparently small gestures of hospitality. The final reward belongs to God, and even the minimum support given to a disciple for identifying him as a follower of Christ will not be forgotten.

scholarViews.insight: The Little Ones of Jesus probably refer to the low social status of the majority of his followers; therefore, a simple gesture of care to them has great value before God.
The twelve were disciples that Jesus gradually raised to the office of apostles and sent; the choice shows that the Lord confers honor and grace in stages, preparing his messengers for the mission.
Jesus seems to have in view of the twelve patriarchs of the ancient tribes of Israel when choosing twelve disciples, linking the mission of the apostles to God's previous plan for his people.

questions: What changes in the way of living when we understand that following Jesus includes being sent by him and not just believing in him privately?
In which situations is it more difficult to confess Christ before people: when there is rejection, fear of losing relationships or pressure to soften the message?
What kind of hospitality or concrete support can I offer today to a servant of Christ, remembering that even a simple gesture counts before God?
study.practice: This week, choose a concrete form of support for someone who serves Christ faithfully: an offering, a meal, a word of encouragement, specific prayer or practical help. At the same time, examine where people's fear has silenced their confession of Jesus. Ask God for the courage to speak clearly, without aggressiveness, and to remain faithful even when the answer is rejected. Also practice Christian hospitality, remembering that God values the little gestures made by recognizing the disciples of Jesus.
study.uncertainty: There is a relevant interpretative limitation in Matthew 10:23, because the notes present two possibilities for the expression about the coming of the Son of Man: a reference to Christ's return to his church or a coming in judgment linked to the destruction of Jerusalem. Moreover, in 10:42 the notes suggest that "these small" can mean the disciples of low social status, but this is an interpretive inference, not an identification explicitly explained by the text itself.
